description: We are the team with a Big desire to learn and enjoy the journey
summary: Space Tinkers is a free browser game where anyone aged 12 and up designs a small satellite (a CubeSat) for a real customer need, such as watching Amazon deforestation or mapping the Moon's south pole, following the six steps NASA uses to design a science mission. Every choice ripples through the whole system: a sharper camera adds mass and power, needs bigger panels, a bigger rocket and more budget, and produces more data than the radio can send. The six resources (mass, power, budget, data, comms and time) are always on screen, and the mission then flies for a year through real space weather recorded by NASA DONKI. The Mission Report explains why the mission succeeded or failed. Players can play solo, guided by a crew of characters with conflicting goals, or as a team of up to four, where each player owns part of the spacecraft and everyone must say GO before launch. The game turns systems thinking, the core skill of real mission teams, into something you can feel and replay.
details:
What it does Space Tinkers lets players build a space mission from scratch and learn that every engineering decision has a cost somewhere else. There are six missions: Amazon deforestation, Cerrado fire scars, urban growth, floods and weather in southern Brazil, a lunar south pole mapper and a small lunar lander. Each mission has at least two different winning designs (checked by an automatic test), so there is no single right answer: players must trade off.

How it works The game follows the six steps of NASA's Design and Develop Science Missions process: (1) Identify Need & Goals: meet the customer and read the goals; (2) Define Concept: choose orbit, launcher and ground station with cockpit controls and a live 3D preview; (3) Define Requirements: flip cards that turn each goal into a measurable number and a way to verify it; (4) Design: pick the instrument, structure, power, attitude control, radio and computer, and watch the ripple effect on all six resources; (5) Build & Verify: a launch checklist, a Go/No-Go vote by the crew, a prediction of how much data will reach Earth, and a choice of launch date; (6) Implement: a staged launch and a one-year mission in 3D, day by day. The six resources (mass, power, budget, data, comms, time) are always visible. Hovering any option previews how it would change each one. The engine checks that the spacecraft mass and orbit fit the chosen rocket; a rocket that should not fly is scrubbed on the pad. During the mission, real geomagnetic storms swell the upper air and pull the orbit down, solar particle events can reset the computer and wear the panels, and memory fills with photos between ground passes. When something happens, mission control calls inside the 3D view and the player has 10 seconds to decide. The same design can succeed in the quiet Sun of 2019 and struggle at the solar maximum of 2024. The Mission Report gives a score and 0 to 3 stars, explains what happened and why, compares the player's prediction with the result and with the previous attempt, and unlocks learning cards based on Peter Senge's laws of systems thinking. "Sources & math" shows every formula with the player's own numbers.

Team mode Up to four players join a room with a 6-letter code. Each takes a role (Mission manager, Payload scientist, Spacecraft engineer, Communications and ground) and can only change the choices of that role, so the conflicts of a real mission team (more science vs. less mass, power, cost and data) become a negotiation. Players talk through quick shouts and a short text chat, and the launch needs GO from every player. Solo players get the same conflict through crew advice from the four characters.

Benefits and goals Good tools exist for single pieces of a mission (orbits, rockets, satellites), but few show how everything connects. Space Tinkers is designed as a "microworld": a safe place to make decisions, see consequences that in real life would be far away in time and space, and reflect on the structure that produced them. It needs no prior knowledge: every number comes with a plain-language sentence, glossary tips and three difficulty levels. It runs in any browser, offline too (with a timeline instead of 3D), in English, Portuguese and Spanish, so it can be used in classrooms, clubs and at home.

Tools and technologies Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no build step; Three.js for the 3D views; PeerJS (WebRTC) for team rooms; WebAudio for sound effects generated live in code; a pure simulation engine (sim.js, life.js) with a Keplerian orbit propagator; automated tests in the browser for the engine, game balance and translations. Hosted on Vercel.
